Slides and notes

Tap any slide to present from there.

Slide 1 · Notes

Keep it light for ten seconds, then go straight to the next slide.

Slide 2 · Notes

Say plainly what you would and wouldn’t have to report. Anyone can step out, no explanation needed.

Slide 3 · Notes

Ask about “kids in this spot,” never “you.” Expect: deciding whether to get in the car, knowing which bills are late, getting siblings fed, scanning a parent in recovery for signs of a slip, guilt about wanting to leave. “The three Cs still hold. Today goes further.”

Slide 4 · Notes

That’s why an essay at 11 p.m. after a fight can feel impossible. Shonkoff and colleagues call severe, long-lasting, unbuffered stress toxic stress, and name the buffer: steady, supportive relationships with adults. That’s what the rest of today is about.

Slide 5 · Notes

Hands for guesses first. Many students guess far lower.

Slide 6 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 7 · Notes

Verhulst, Neale and Kendler (2015). Ask: “Which part surprised you?” Many expect “I’ll turn out like them.”

Slide 8 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 9 · Notes

Werner followed children on Kauai from birth. The outcome isn’t fixed.

Slide 10 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 11 · Notes

The rules protect the secret and leave kids alone with it. The roles are ways of coping, and they can become a box. In many families and cultures, teens helping run the household is normal and a source of pride; the concern is when it costs sleep, school or friends, or nobody looks after you in return. Relapse is common in recovery and not a failure of the kid.

Slide 12 · Notes

Two minutes. Keep it about a made-up friend.

Slide 13 · Notes

Take a few. Skip: “Just leave,” “My uncle was worse,” or telling everyone.

Slide 14 · Notes

Ask: what might Jordan be feeling, and afraid of? Ideas: exhausted, embarrassed, protective of their mom, scared of what happens if anyone finds out.

Slide 15 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 16 · Notes

When should the friend tell an adult anyway? If Jordan is being hurt, not being fed or cared for, in a car with an impaired driver, or talking about not wanting to be here.

Slide 17 · Notes

The answer. Let the room react before you move on.

Slide 18 · Notes

Narcan has been over the counter since 2023. Alateen and NACoA are for teens affected by someone else’s use. Heritability is a real reason to be careful with your own use, without shame.

Slide 19 · Notes

Privately, on the card: an adult at school, someone in family or community, where they’d go if they had to leave fast, and two backup ride numbers. Nobody shares.

Slide 20 · Notes

Group composition matters; check who is in the room. If a student says a parent relapsed, recovery and relapse are both part of the story.

Slide 21 · Notes

Share the take-home link. Invite anyone to check in one on one. Follow your reporting rules.

If you want more

The full plan, care notes, and research. None of it is needed to teach the lesson.

Lesson plan

A suggested plan. Change the timing, skip or reorder slides, or use any part on its own. You know your students.

Goal

Students learn what living with unpredictability does to the stress system, that risk is real and the outcome isn't fixed, the roles and unspoken rules families fall into, and six moves for support on their own terms. Nobody is asked about their own family.

Materials

  • The deck on the big screen. Each slide carries its own point, so no script is needed.
  • Index cards, one per student
  • Pens
  • The take-home link to share afterward

Flow

  1. 3 minBefore we start, and the three Cs
  2. 3 minA stress system that never stands down
  3. 5 minThree research guesses
  4. 3 minRules and roles
  5. 3 minTurn and talk, share out
  6. 4 minJordan, and the promise
  7. 4 minSix moves, your support map, close

One on one (about 15 minutes)

The three Cs, the three research guesses, Jordan, and the support map.

Before you teach
Group composition.

A group of students who share this experience can be powerful, and it can also out someone. Talk with each student individually before placing them, and let them choose.

Say your reporting rules first.

Telling you that a parent drinks isn't the same as a report; the question is whether the student is safe and cared for. Say that clearly, and invite "If I tell you something, what would you have to share?"

Keep it about Jordan.

Even in a group of students who know why they're there, keep the discussion on Jordan and the research. Personal detail belongs in individual time.

Recovery and relapse.

Some students have a parent in recovery and live scanning for signs of a slip. Name relapse as common in recovery, and never theirs to catch or prevent.

Their own use.

With family history, the step from coping to pattern is shorter. Invite students to say it if they notice it, framed as strength, not confession.

Practical safety.

The ride rule and overdose basics are concrete and often new. Make sure every student leaves with two backup ride numbers.

Every student in the room

Culture, family, identity, ability and money: what to keep in mind for this topic.

Helping at home is cultural.

In many families teens caring for siblings or running the household is normal and valued. Present parentification as a line about cost, not a judgment about any family's way of doing things.

Distrust of agencies.

Some families have immigration worries or past bad experiences with systems. Those concerns make sense; name that a student can decide how much to share and when.

Family structure.

The person using may be a parent, a stepparent, a grandparent, an older sibling or a partner of a parent. Keep language open to every household.

Faith communities.

For some students a faith leader or congregation is the first adult and the steadiest support. Include them on the support map.

Money and work.

Some students work to cover gaps at home or are managing bills. Mention that counselors can help with college applications and aid forms when a parent can't.

Stigma differs.

In some families addiction is spoken of openly; in others it's deeply shameful. Let students use whatever words they're comfortable with.

What the research says

About 19 million US kids, roughly 1 in 4, live with a parent who has a substance use disorder; alcohol is the most common.

McCabe et al., JAMA Pediatrics, 2025

Stress that's severe, long-lasting and not buffered by support is called toxic stress. Steady, supportive relationships with adults buffer it best.

Shonkoff, Garner et al., Pediatrics, 2012

Pooling twin and adoption studies, alcohol use disorder is about 50% heritable; the rest comes from environment, stress and experience.

Verhulst, Neale and Kendler, Psychological Medicine, 2015

Following children of parents with alcoholism in Kauai from birth, most had not developed serious problems by 18. Those who did well into adulthood had leaned on more sources of support: extended family, neighbors and school.

Werner, Journal of Studies on Alcohol, 1986 · Werner and Johnson, Substance Use & Misuse, 2004

Naloxone (Narcan) has been sold without a prescription since 2023.

US Food and Drug Administration, 2023
